utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no objection, and we would only like a brief time to reply to the response, if permitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Of course. No doubt. The only problem I see is that if it would be in fact exculpatory material, it would be without any time limit that these documents or exhibits have to be disclosed to the Defence immediately, and it's not a question of a motion. Therefore, I would really ask the Prosecution to reconsider this issue. We are not confronted with a request under Rule 127, but it's the Prosecution's obligation to act proprio motu whenever they come across with material that tends to be exculpatory. So therefore, the one -- the motion and the response to the motion doesn't exclude the other obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Certainly we agree, but it is our position that this is not Rule 68 material, and that is what the response would address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I understand. Just for a point of clarification: The OTP, in essence, is saying that there is no Rule 68 material in connection with Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we shouldn't have a dispute on this issue at the moment. I only wanted to emphasise that if there is material tending to be exculpatory notwithstanding that no doubt there is a time period of 14 days for answering your motion, there is still this obligation, and later on we will see whether this material is exculpatory or not. I understand it's not only in our case this team working on this is confronted with the same problem. Let's come back to our concrete case. As usual, what about protective measures, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's my understanding with respect to this witness, number 72, she has sought no protective measures. However, there are a couple of points and topics that we'll be asking, when the time is appropriate during her testimony, that we go into closed session because she's uncomfortable, quite candidly, to identify certain individuals in open session, and it's her view, based on the representations that she shared with me, that she did not get the approval of those individuals to identify them in open court. So she has asked at that point that we go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If I then may only ask you to concentrate the line of questions in closed session to one point in time that we don't have to go in and out of closed session. So there is no impediment to ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I then ask you to give us your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I start?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let me repeat directly our apologies that you had to wait for such a long time. It was not foreseeable that another witness would take us such a long period of time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But now the time has come, and it's for the Defence to start the examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Ostojic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ma'am. My name is John Ostojic, and along with Branko Lukic and Danilo Cirkovic, we represent Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Stoja, and my last name is Radakovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have or do you go by any nickname?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have a nickname. It is Mica, and people tend to use my nickname more than my first name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, ma'am, where do you presently reside?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: I presently reside in Prijedor, in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long have you lived in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: I've lived in Prijedor since 1963.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Forgive me for asking; can you please tell us your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: My date of birth is 13 July 1946.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And forgive me also for asking, ma'am; can you tell us what your marital status is.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm divorced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As it relates, at least in my view, in connection with some testimony you're going to give to us this afternoon, can you tell us how long you've been divorced.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: I've been divorced for 30 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have a child who was four months old when I got divorced. My son is now 30 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving along in my outline, can you share with us your educational background and tell us what is the highest level of education that you have attained.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: After the elementary school, I went to an administrative school in Belgrade, and I became a typist. That's what I completed. And I started working in Prijedor municipality in 1963, and later on, I continued my education, my secondary education, and I ended up being an administrative technician after completing my secondary education.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And describe for us, if you can, what are the duties and obligations of an administrative technician.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't describe the duties of an administrative technician but of a technical secretary, yes. A technical secretary is a person, a man or a woman, who usually works as a secretary to a higher official, depending on the position, in a certain organisation or institution. My job was as a technical secretary in the Municipal Assembly, and I served as a secretary to the president of the Assembly and the vice-president of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So to speed the time line up a little bit, in 1991 through 1992, you worked as the technical secretary in the Municipal Assembly for both the president and the vice-president; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during that time period, did you in fact work with a man by the name of Professor Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. His full name was Muhamed Cehajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Muhamed Cehajic, at the time that you worked at the Municipal Assembly, what position did he hold?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cehajic was the president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that same time period, did you have an opportunity to work with Dr. Milomir Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. During that same period of time when Cehajic -- Mr. Cehajic became president, Mr. Stakic became vice-president of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during that time period up through and including the 30th of April, 1992, you worked for both of them; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. I worked for both of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Describe for us, ma'am, if you recall, the relationship between Mr. Cehajic and Dr. Stakic during and including the period in which you worked for both of them.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: The contact, i.e., the relationship, between Mr. Cehajic and Mr. Stakic was very serious and very correct; they cooperated, and that happened very often. My office was between their two offices. They would cross my office to go into each other's office, upon invitation or spontaneously. I didn't notice that they would have any disagreements or similar things between them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that period of time that you worked --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that period of time that you worked for both Mr. Cehajic and Dr. Stakic, did Dr. Stakic exhibit any ill will against Mr. Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I never noticed anything like that. I don't know what they talked about when they were in each other's offices, but as far as I could see and observe, their contacts and their communication in my office was always correct, serious. Their relationship was perfect, if one may put it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any time did Dr. Stakic, based on your personal observations and recollections, did he ever tell you that he disliked Mr. Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. And vice versa. Maybe I am now anticipating your question, but no, he didn't say anything like that. On the contrary, he would say, "I am going with Muhamed," "I have an agreement with Muhamed," and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so I can understand your position, could you describe for me your day-to-day duties while you were at the Municipal Assembly during the period of time that you worked for Mr. Cehajic and Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: It was a period somewhat different to the periods before, different because options were different. There was a multi-party management or leadership, and that was very much different. Cehajic represented the SDA, and Stakic represented the SDS. So at that time I had somewhat less work because they relied a bit more on their respective parties. But I still discharged the duties of a technical secretary. I received their visitors, I referred them to one of the two of them, I talked to the visitors, and if I had to refer them to somebody else, I would do that and I would explain why I had to do that. I also answered their telephones, I would connect them if they had a call, and that also, obviously, depended on whether they wanted to talk to the person who wanted to talk to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you, ma'am, during that time period, do any actual typing or stenography work for either of the two gentlemen?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't do either. I stopped doing that when I started working in their office. This was not in my job description, so I didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me take you briefly, sticking with the theme of your employment and your job duties, to the period of April 30, 1992 through approximately September 30, 1992. Were your job responsibilities and duties the same as they were prior to April 30th when you worked with Mr. Cehajic and Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the same. As much as it was requested of me by the visitors who came to visit, either one of them. So I did more or less the same things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so that I understand your testimony correctly, after April 30, 1992, you likewise did not type or perform any stenography tasks for Dr. Stakic all the way through the time that you worked there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. I did not have to type one single letter. I couldn't do it; I didn't have a typewriter. If I wanted to do that, I would have to go to another office, I would have to type there. That would mean that somebody would have to replace me in my regular job, and we had different people who did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Taking you briefly to the period of 1991 and 1992, did you, ma'am, experience or have any family members who became refugees and moved from the area of Croatia to the Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My sister came in 1990 from Zagreb, her husband and two children. They were working for an auto transport firm in Zagreb and then they came to Prijedor and began working there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what year was that, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: That was 1990, end of 1990. In 1991, they already finished their house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Forgive me for having to ask you the following series of questions, but so that I, as well as the other members of this Chamber and courtroom can have a better understanding of you as a person, did you, madam, at any time have any ill will, prejudice, hatred, or discrimination against Muslims, Croats, or other non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Me personally?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, never. I -- I never felt any need to discriminate against any other ethnic groups. They didn't treat me that way, and I didn't treat them that way. I'm referring here to my neighbours and to my workmates, starting with my superior, Cehajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you, madam, still maintain relationships and friendships with members of different ethnic groups, such as Muslim, Croatian, and non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I still do. I have a wonderful relationship with my non-Serb neighbours. And at work too, I have a close friend who is a Croat, a lady friend. I'm not sure if that matters, but she lives in Zagreb. I think she is as close to me as my sister is. Sometimes I feel even closer to her. I don't have that much to talk about with my sister. We usually discuss problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also let me ask a couple more personal questions: In connection with your 30-year-old son, is he presently married?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your ethnic background, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: I am a Serb, but I've only known this since 1991. I've only been aware of this since 1991, because prior to that period of time, no one had even thought to mention that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your ex-husband, the father of your son, what is his ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: He's a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now your son, being the son of two Serbs, as you put it, being currently married, can you tell us whether he's married to a Serb, Croat, Muslim, or another non-Serb?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: My son is married to a Croatian woman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to switch the topic here a little bit. If I may be permitted to just switch the topic a little bit, ma'am. I'm going to ask you, during the period of time --

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. During the period of time that you worked at the Municipal Assembly, specifically in the early 1990s, 1991 through 1992, was there a position in the Municipal Assembly that was known as mayor, or was it the only position that was identified as president of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. At the Municipal Assembly, up to three years ago, the position of mayor never existed. There was only the president of the assembly. We've had a mayor perhaps for the last three or four years, as far as I can remember. I had the honour to work with the first mayor for six months, after which I retired. And I think the position of mayor is very, very different from the position of president of the Municipal Assembly, in terms of their authority, in terms of their areas of competence, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Permit me to ask you this, and that is, could in 1991 and 1992, the president of the Municipal Assembly fire, discharge, or dismiss you from your employment that you held?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. That would take a major violation, and then there would be a disciplinary committee which would decide. There had to be some proof of what I had done, and then maybe I would have been moved to a different position. But this never happened to anyone. At least, that's what I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is true, then, that Mr. Cehajic, during the period that he was president of the Municipal Assembly, had no authority or competencies to discharge or fire you from your employment; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he could move me from one job to another, perhaps, or bring -- give a proposal for someone else to be put, to be brought into my place for reasons that I cannot speculate about. Likewise, I find myself unable to speculate as to what he might have done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to speculate on what he might have done. With respect to the tenure that you held with the mayor of Prijedor, this new function that arose three or so years ago, did the mayor have the competence and the authority to discharge a person in your function and position in the Municipal Assembly building?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The mayor did have the authority, and he could discharge me or anyone else who worked for the Municipal Assembly. He had control over the whole institution, that means, over the whole community. And he need not have given any reasons. Decisions would be made and people would be moved from one job to another. So it was an unpleasant situation, an uncomfortable situation for all those who were there, because they would just be removed, and they didn't even have the right to ask questions to know why. They had told us in advance that once the mayor was in place, he wouldn't ask any questions. He could just fire you, as simple as that, draw up a decision and fire you. I didn't myself read the rules, so I don't know anything about the details of the mayor's authority apart from what I've told you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, at your request, I advised the Court that we may be seeking leave to go into closed session on a couple of topics. Right before, or in the next few minutes I'm going to be asking to go into closed session. However, I'd like to lay the foundation and groundwork so that the Court has an appreciation and then we'll go into closed session and I'll continue to ask you a couple of questions. First, ma'am, tell us approximately the time period - just the time period - when you were first asked to testify in this case.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: The time period, the first time I was asked that, was July last year. I was back from vacation. It may have been at some point after the 20th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell us, if you will, when the Defence team asked you to potentially be a witness and appear before this Court in the Stakic matter.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: It was a day or two before New Year. So it hasn't even been a month. I was addressed by Mr. Branko Lukic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at your request and with the Court's approval, I'd like to go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Confirmed. Can you please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, I'm going to take you to a period of time approximately ten years ago. I'm going to ask you to attempt to recall certain facts and observations that you made and experiences that you had in that time period. By way of background, I understand completely that specific dates are difficult to remember, so I will attempt, with the Court's permission and no objection from the OTP, to set forth certain time lines and ask that you accept them as being, for our purposes at least, accurate. My question in essence is: On April 30, 1992, which is the date, I think, the takeover in the Prijedor municipality occurred, can you share with us, from whom did you hear about this take-over?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard about the takeover in the morning. I was getting ready to go to work, and a neighbour called me on the phone. This friend of mine, she is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is it that she advised you of when she called you on or about that date?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: It was in the morning, and she said, "Do you know that the Serbs took over?" I said, "I have no idea. I just woke up minutes ago. I'm getting ready to go to work. I'll just go there and see what happens." That was the whole conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And subsequently, ma'am, were you able to go to the Municipal Assembly building and see what had happened?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: I went to the Municipal Assembly building. I went to work as usual. There were no apparent changes. However, standing at the door of the Municipal Assembly, I saw two young men in uniform. They ID'd me. They wanted to see my ID. I showed them my ID, and they said, "Okay. It's okay. You can enter the building."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The period of time immediately following the takeover on the 30th of April, 1992, did you have an opportunity to see Dr. Milomir Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him in the office in which he sat even before the takeover.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Dr. Stakic remained in the same office he had held prior to the takeover?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Very briefly. A day, two or three, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss or have a conversation with Dr. Stakic about the takeover?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Never. I never discussed such things with my superiors. I never discussed issues related to their positions. And I'm talking about all the presidents that I worked with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the way, I'm curious to know; how many different presidents of the Municipal Assembly had you worked for in your 30-plus year career?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Thirteen or 14, I believe. I should try counting them to give you the exact figure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, that's approximately. Thank you. Now, your relationship with Dr. Stakic was obviously professional, and as you described, he would not, and certainly you would not, have any discussions relating to things that would concern his position and necessarily things that would be relevant to your position; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. We never discussed Dr. Stakic's business except if he wanted me to make a phone call or to call someone from another service in the institution or someone from the administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to take you through the time period that we've, in essence, attempted to establish, and that is the time period from April 30th through May 30, 1992. And ma'am, I'm using and asking you to also have an understanding of May 30th as being the attack on the city of Prijedor. During that time period but before the attack on Prijedor, you as the receptionist who received telephone calls for Dr. Stakic at the Municipal Assembly building, did you likewise during that time period receive telephone calls from Mr. Cehajic, asking to speak to Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That was a day or two or three, perhaps maybe only a day. I find this difficult to speak about, the exact time. It's been 10 or 12 years since. Myself, I was very unhappy about the whole thing, what was going on, and it's difficult for me to speak about these moments. But yes, I do remember Cehajic calling. He said,"Mica, can you please put me through to Dr. Stakic. I need to have a word." So I put him through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Dr. Stakic --

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Then they had a conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was my question. Thank you. I think you've answered, but just so I'm clear -- yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just for clarification, on the transcript, it reads, "Yes, that was a day or three perhaps," but what does it mean? Sorry. After the takeover or --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll clarify it, Your Honour. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, it's my fault and I probably interrupted you and I should not have, so I apologise for that. Is it your testimony that soon after 30th of April [Realtime transcript read in error "May"] 1992, the day of the takeover, Mr. Cehajic called Dr. Stakic and you put him through and they had a conversation; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. First he called me and asked me to put him through to Dr. Stakic because he couldn't call him directly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're still having -- and madam thank you for your answer, but we're still having trouble. Perhaps because it's my fault. It says in the transcript, "after May 30th." I think the question was specific. I think we said April 30th; the transcript says May 30th. I just want to be clear, so can I have one more attempt at this, Judge? In any event, ma'am, the transcript says after May 30th. My question, I believe, was confined to April 30th. Let me just please be permitted to ask you the question one more time, I'll endeavour to say it slowly so everybody can get it, although it's not necessarily a major point. After the takeover, April 30th, 1992, did you in fact, ma'am, have an opportunity to receive a call from Mr. Cehajic seeking to talk to Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: After the takeover - now I must add it was the 30th of April - I put Mr. Cehajic through to Dr. Stakic, because Mr. Cehajic had requested to speak to Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before you put someone through, from my understanding of your position, you would contact Dr. Stakic and advise him who was on the phone, who was looking for him, and then if he agreed to accept the call, you would transfer the call to Dr. Stakic; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would dial Dr. Stakic in that case, and I would tell him, "You have Mr. Cehajic waiting on the line." And then Mr. Stakic would tell me, "Okay, put him through." And then I would put him through and they would continue their conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's the way your function was essentially before as it was after April 30, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. That's always been my job and my task.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Dr. Stakic at that time refuse to accept the call of Mr. Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. He never had a moment's doubt even.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the period of time April 30, 1992, through May 30, 1992, based on your personal observations and experiences, did Dr. Stakic at any time during that limited time period in any way defame or render negative or discriminatory comments against Mr. Cehajic or anyone?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not for a moment during the period you referred to. Dr. Stakic never for a moment showed any sign of ill will to any citizen, or any non-Serb citizens, for that matter, Muslims or Croats. Quite the contrary. I believe I don't remember that someone came and Dr. Stakic refused to see him. But there were still people working there, being gainfully employed at the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving now quickly to the period of May 30, 1992, which was an attack on the city town of Prijedor, and madam, I know that you're familiar with the events that transpired on May 22 at Hambarine as well as May 24th at Kozarac, but I think for our purposes we'll limit your testimony specifically, since you lived in the town of Prijedor, and describe for us what it is that you experienced on or about May 30, 1992.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 30th of May, that's when the attack on Prijedor took place by Muslims. How did I find out? It was 5.00 in the morning. There was sounds of shooting in the town. We thought should we get up quickly and go anywhere. I know father said, "Come on, get up quickly," and I said, "Oh, come on, just leave me be," but no matter. My neighbour called from the adjacent building. She could hear more clearly where the shooting was coming from. Sometimes it's difficult to tell, because in a town the shooting echoes because the buildings are close together. And then she told me that her daughter-in-law called, who lived close to the secondary school for economics, in that district, and she said there was a man lying on the ground, a wounded man outside her building. Later, we found out that this was a bread delivery man, because they are the earlier risers. I didn't realise that anything else was happening or why there was shooting. I only knew what I learned over the phone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Specifically in connection with this attack on the city town of Prijedor, I would like to ask you the following question, that is: Within the city town, is there a mosque, a Muslim house of worship within the city town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: There was a mosque in the centre of Prijedor, if that is the way I can put it. I don't know what the centre is. But in any case, there was a mosque there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the attack on Prijedor by the Muslims, as you've described them, was the mosque, the Muslim place of worship, destroyed?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The mosque was destroyed on the eve of the 12th of July. Why do I remember the date? Because -- now I'm going to sidetrack a little. I was born on St. Peter's Day, but it has been recorded I was born on the 13th. That's why my birthday is on the 13th, and that's why I thought I had a fireworks display on the eve of my birthday. That's how I can -- but my birthday proper. So on the 11th of July, on the eve of my birthday proper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so we have it clear on the record, my question was - and I'll repeat it - the mosque was not destroyed or defaced or burned on the 30th of May, 1992 or at any time from the 30th of April, 1992, up until the time that you recall, namely July 12, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't destroyed. One could see it, passing by, and I saw that scene from my balcony. We were watching it for a long time. It wasn't a short thing. It lasted for a long period of time. I don't know why, but in any case, there were -- I don't know. There were things burning for a long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me move to a different area specifically relating to Dr. Stakic. At any time did you personally observe or experience whether or not Dr. Stakic exhibited prejudice, hatred, discrimination, or ill will against Muslims, Croats, or non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: I never noticed that. Dr. Stakic was very correct in his behaviour towards everybody. Whoever came, he would receive them. He never said anything against Croats or Muslims in front of me, or any other person, for that matter. I believe that he was very correct towards all the ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, although I've had the personal pleasure of meeting you over the last couple of days, I'm going to ask you a question: Would you have worked for Dr. Stakic if he had exhibited any such signs or propensity of hatred, prejudice, discrimination, or ill will towards other ethnic groups, namely Muslims, Croats, and non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: I would not have worked for him or anybody else. And even if, for example, Cehajic had said something against a Serb, I would have told him, "Don't say that in front of me." I would have reacted the same way if Dr. Stakic said something like that. But Dr. Stakic helped everybody who came asking for help, and I didn't notice ever that Dr. Stakic would turn down something that he had to do on that day, that he needed to do for people on any given day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And likewise, ma'am, am I correct that if you knew or heard about the fact that Dr. Stakic allegedly was discriminatory, had prejudices or ill will or hatred toward other ethnic groups, in fact you would not be here testifying; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't testify. Never. I'm sure that Dr. Stakic, as far as I could see and observe, and I believe that I was old enough and experienced enough in order to be able to judge a person and see what people think, because I've had a number of people or presidents of the municipality that I worked with, and I think I would have noticed any little gesture that would point to the fact that he showed intolerance against anybody. But he was really kind and polite towards everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask Defence counsel, please, to refrain from hypothetical questions and, by doing so, misleading the witness, because from the transcript it transpires now the impression that the witness would not be prepared, on request, to testify when there would be another testimony at stake. So therefore, please take care.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to a different issue and time period that we've identified in essence as being the spring and summer of 1992, I'm going to ask for your personal experiences and observations for that time period, essentially from April 30, 1992, through September 30, 1992. Can you tell us whether or not Milomir Stakic had any influence or power and authority over the police in the Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic did not have any influence or power or authority over the police in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Share with us, if you will, what is the basis of your opinion and your personal experience?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: My personal experience consists in the following: In 1992, I went to see Mr. Drljaca and ask him for a favour, and the favour was for my son to be -- not to be sent to the war. I didn't ask that favour of Dr. Stakic because I knew that he was not in the position to do that. Mr. Drljaca did not grant my request.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the period the spring and summer of 1992, can you share with us who your son's best friend was at that time.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Spring and summer 1992, my son -- I'm not clear about your question, but he did have a friend at the time who -- whose name was Nedzad Kosuran.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a point in time that your son discussed his friend with you and the fact that he was detained in Omarska in 1992, approximately June; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I just wanted to correct myself, and I wanted to say that they were not acquainted just for a brief period of time. They were friends from high school. They shared the same bench in the high school. They were sitting together. And my son came to me and asked me for advice, and he said, "Nedzko is in Omarska. He was taken there for investigation, for interrogation." And I gave it a long and hard thought. I love my son. I wanted to help him. As simple as that. And I also like his friend who came to our house very often. And I was thinking about maybe going to Stakic, but I knew that that was out of the question. Then I went to see my ex-husband, who worked as an inspector, as an investigator. I don't know what to call that. I didn't find that very easy. I'm not finding it easy now to have to talk about it openly, because we had interrupted all of our ties 20 years before that, and the only times we would talk to each other were when we were in court, when I would sue him for child support. That's when we talked. But I had to swallow my pride, and I had to go and see him. I went to see him together with my son, of course. We didn't have much to say to each other. Our only topic of conversation was this young man. He asked me how I knew that. And although my son was there, I had to speak on his behalf, and I had to say that our son knew the boy very well and that he wanted to help him and that that had nothing whatsoever to do with any problems in Prijedor. And he said, "Very well, then. Okay." And that lad was then transferred to Trnopolje and there he stayed for I don't know how long, but what mattered to me was that he eventually was released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, just so I understand, instead of going to your colleague at work, someone who you have known for a period of time, someone who you obviously didn't have any conflict with, namely Dr. Stakic, instead you chose to inquire about this young man of your ex-husband with whom you've had a bitter divorce and an ongoing bitter relationship; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't go to Dr. Stakic for a simple reason: I knew that he didn't have any contacts with the police and that the police usually did their job, and they are independent in their work. Sometimes I used to say that the police is a state within the state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am now turning to a different but somewhat related topic. During that same time period, the spring and summer of 1992, based upon your personal experiences and observations, can you tell us whether or not Milomir Stakic had any influence, power, or authority over the military, whether it be the JNA or the VRS?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I have an example to share with you and by which to show you that Dr. Stakic couldn't influence them. In any case, he didn't grant my request. I entered Dr. Stakic's office, and I asked him whether he could help me with -- again I'm talking about my son, because that is what I always go back to, because I've always lived for my son. To this very day and all throughout the war, my only concern was his well-being, where he was going, where he would be sent. Because even before that, I was under the impression of the war events -- my son served his compulsory military service in Karlovac in 1990 and 1991. So already at the time, I was stressed out, and I really was concerned with what would happen next. So let me go back to my request to the -- what I started talking about. I entered Dr. Stakic's office and I asked him if he could help me by relieving my son of his compulsory military service. I knew that he couldn't help me because everybody had to serve in the army, but I had to try. I had to give it my best shot so that one day I could say at least I had given a shot, I had tried. So I addressed Dr. Stakic because of that. Then I also told him --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Then I also told him what is it that I wanted to see him about, and I asked him if it was possible to grant my son's request not to be sent to the front line. And his answer was, "Unfortunately, I can't do that. I don't have any influence over the army. If I did, then I would do something like that for my wife whose brother is being sent to the front line, or some other of my family who are either being sent or who are there already."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, ma'am --

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Fortunately --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think the interpreter said "fortunately" and I think the witness may have said "unfortunately" but that was because of my interruption. May I be permitted to put a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, did you come to learn about Dr. Stakic's personal family; namely, his wife's brother - his brother-in-law - and the son of his wife's sister? What fate did they ultimately have as a result of being in the military in 1992?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: When I said "unfortunately," I wanted to continue. Later on, in 1992, towards the end of that year - I can't remember the date - Bozana's brother, Mr. Stakic's wife's brother, was killed, and also his sister's husband. So it was indeed true that Stakic didn't have any influence over the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a couple of questions in connection with Dr. Stakic's family and the personal observations and experiences that you had with them. Did you have an opportunity to meet his young son?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: I met him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And share with us the circumstances in which you met him.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: The first time I saw lady Bozana with her son was in 1991. Mr. Cehajic was already there, and they met each other in the corridor in front of my office. They greeted each other very cordially, and Mr. Cehajic was very polite and pleasant to her. That was my first contact with her -- that is, with them. Later on when they moved to Prijedor and when they took residence there, Milan, the son, Dr. Stakic's son, went to kindergarten, and sometimes Dr. Stakic would pick him up from the kindergarten and would bring him back to the office and I would mind him while Dr. Stakic still had work to do. And that was the -- the lad was really nice, and he would sometimes peek through the keyhole to see what his father was doing in the adjacent office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, share with us -- ma'am, please share with us your opinion relating to Dr. Stakic's character and reputation.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: I perceived Dr. Stakic as -- as a people's man, a man that belonged to the people. He was well educated. He communicated well with the people. He helped people. Very diligent, very responsible, hard-working person. And if that was not my perception of Dr. Stakic, if I didn't have such an opinion of him, believe me, I wouldn't be here for a single moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, ma'am, what your thoughts, feelings, and emotions were at or about the time that Dr. Stakic was arrested and brought here to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: When I heard that on television, I was quite surprised. I was actually frozen, because, as I say, I was really surprised and depressed to hear that. I definitely, firmly believed that he should not have been taken there. And I thought if he had to be taken, then he would have been taken earlier on. And I was absolutely convinced that it was just an accident, a sheer accident, and not for a single moment did I think that this was the right thing to do. And to this very day, I still believe that it must have been a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We have no further questions. Thank you, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To be honest, I'm taken by surprise when I reflect your amended proffer. You didn't cover all the issues included there. Is it on purpose or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes. Quite frankly, I can explain if the Court wishes. The proffer, as the Court has requested us to turn in, is to obtain information that the witness may have. The Defence, however, we believe, is placing this witness on the stand specifically for certain issues. We certainly don't want to mislead or misrepresent that the witness has information in connection with other issues that may interest - although we don't agree - interest other parties in this case. We brought her specifically for the items that I believe she testified consistent with. So -- but she does have that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for all this clarification, and I think it's then appropriate to have the break now. The Prosecution is prepared for cross-examination immediately after the break or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sure. I can either start now or after the break. Ten minutes, if you want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then the trial stays adjourned until ten minutes past three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. May I ask that we can have a calculation and also ask the registry to be prepared. What about your estimate, you will need?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I think at least two hours, so I do not anticipate finishing today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: From -- so that nobody is taken by surprise, it will be a long testimony, and there will be a long line of questions tomorrow, and also, therefore, it might even be that, if necessary and in order to enable the witness to return tomorrow, that we have to proceed longer as scheduled on the basis of the evident questions to put to you. But only that you know. Please start.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examined by Mr. Koumjian:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, thank you for agreeing to come to The Hague at the request of the Defence and to tell us what you know about these events. Madam, you described Dr. Stakic's character towards the end of your direct testimony and called him well-educated and diligent and responsible. Would you agree -- would you describe him as a very intelligent man?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you describe him as a hard-working president of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Dr. Stakic a person who was firm in his beliefs or was he the type of person who would be manipulated by other people?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: I think Dr. Stakic stood by his beliefs, and I don't think he could have been manipulated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us more about how you know or how long you knew Dr. Stakic. Would it -- did you know him before he became the vice-president of the elected multi-ethnic Assembly?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: The first time I saw the president, or the vice-president at this time, when he came to the office as the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly. I did not know him or seen him prior to that point. Moreover, I had never even heard of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Well, I know that he was elected following the 1990 elections. Perhaps you can remind me the date when those individuals took office. Do you remember when it was that the persons elected the president and the vice-president of the Assembly following the elections actually took their positions?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: The president of the Assembly, I can't remember the date, but we'd been working up to a year and a half, I think, roughly before the takeover. That's at least what I remember. Now, why is it that I can't remember the exact date? During this time, and I must repeat this, my son was in the army, and I often went there to visit him. That's as long as I could. There was a period where I was not able to go. So I mostly worried about these things, when to go and how to arrive there, what the situation was like in Croatia, would I be able to go and visit my son.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's certainly understandable that you don't remember exact dates. Would it be safe for us to assume that you met Dr. Stakic, that he took that position by at least January of 1991?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. 1991, that's possible. That's roughly what I think too, a year and a half. Yes, that's possible. I don't know. I'm not sure. I don't know the date. I don't know the year, but I think that up to this point, we had been working together for a year and a half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that answer. And when you say a year and a half, you're talking about a year and a half before the takeover of the municipality and when Dr. Stakic took over the office of Mr. --

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Cehajic; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking about this period, because you asked how long before that point in time I had known Mr. Stakic, and the answer is for a year and a half, when he was the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And then he remained in that position, the former position of Professor Cehajic, until January of 1993; is that correct? Are my dates correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the dates. I know that after that, there were some circumstances which led -- which led to Dr. Stakic's removal, but I don't know really. I was never involved in politics. I was never interested in politics, and I never understood politics. My job was to sit there, receive messages, and do what I would be told to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And then I gather from your answer you never attended -- or correct me if I'm wrong; did you ever attend any meetings of political parties?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I never attended a single meeting of any political party, nor was I ever a member of any political party. And you can only attend such meetings if you're a member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that helpful information. Madam, since apparently I understand that you remained in the position of that secretary until after the Dayton Accords, is it correct that you again worked for Dr. Stakic when he came back as the president of the municipality at the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I stayed in the same job. It's a very technical job. It's not any sort of high office or anything. Yes, I kept working in the same job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. We understand that. But perhaps you can help us. Can you tell us, to the best of your recollection, the dates that Dr. Stakic held the office of president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor for the second time?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the dates, but I know that it was in 1995 and 1996. It didn't mean much to me, when someone comes and when someone goes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Would it be correct that he took the position before the end of the war, before the signing of the Dayton Accords?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: I see that I made a mistake. No, not before the signing of the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be correct, then, that he was in the position from 1996 to 1997?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember this because I had some personal trouble. This is what I always relate to when I think about time. I had asked some people who worked in our building to grant me permission for something, and I think it was about the same time. And I think I even asked Dr. Stakic, but to no effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry, but I'm a bit confused about your answer. Is that how you remember the day that he took the position or how you remember the day he left the position?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: It was the period that he was there. I'm not talking about the day he came back or the day he left again. I'm referring to the whole second period that he was in office. For example, the request that I filed, it was in June, and the next year, in April, I was granted approval. So what I know for sure is that throughout that period I've just specified, he was there, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. From at least June 1996 through April of 1997; is that correct? At least through that period of time?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: I'd say yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I understand from your testimony you don't recall the date that Dr. Stakic stopped being the president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, but I'd like you to relate it to another event that I'm sure you recall. Do you recall the day that Mr. Kovacevic was arrested and that Mr. Drljaca was killed during an attempted arrest?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: I do recall those days. It was in the summer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would the date of the 10th of July, 1997, sound approximately correct for when that event occurred?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: That's possible. Again, I know that it was just before St. Peter's Day. Again, this is a personal reference because I was born on that day. That's why I seem to remember. During this period of time, I was not at work. I had a health problem. I had been on sick leave for almost two months. Before and after that, and I had a visitor from abroad visiting me, so that was another reason why I needed to stay home throughout that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you came back to work, was Dr. Stakic still coming to work as the president of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why he stopped coming to work as the president of the Municipal Assembly in the summer of 1997?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, you worked for many presidents of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, and we all would like to take advantage of your great experience. In your experience, is it important for a person in that position to know that is going on throughout the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Not necessarily. For my job, it certainly isn't very important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not talking about your job. I'm talking about the position of president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. Do you think a good president of the Municipal Assembly keeps him or herself informed of what is going on in the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me object to the form of the question, Your Honour, because it obviously calls for a speculative answer. Since this witness has never held that position and counsel is putting in a verb such as "good" president as opposed to maybe average or the best president. So it's not only improper in form but it also calls and speaks for speculative testimony from a witness who did not hold that position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Perhaps you can rephrase the question because the purpose of the question is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, did Dr. Stakic, when he occupied the office of president of the municipality, did he bother to keep himself informed of events in the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Did he bother? It's not up to me to know whether he wanted to keep himself informed or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Madam, you sat outside his office for a period of several years; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You received the phone calls that came to him in his office and passed them on to him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And correct me if I'm wrong, would you also contact individuals on his behalf? In other words, make the outgoing phone call and connect those persons to Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would bring him material that he needed in order to perform his job, such as official journals such as the Gazette, the Official Gazette of Prijedor, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, that's not true. There were other people who were in charge of this, mail, that sort of thing, forwarding documents to Dr. Stakic. That wasn't my job. I was only in charge of my phone, my pen, and my paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you pass on material that came from the mail personnel to Dr. Stakic, or would a mail person walk into the office of the president?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A mail person or a person working in a different section would come. First they would announce their arrival and ask if Dr. Stakic was free to see them, and then the president would either say yes or postpone this, in which case whoever needed to see the president officially would come, bringing the mail or the documents, and they would walk straight into his office to deliver the papers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Dr. Stakic receive, for example, Kozarski Vjesnik whenever it came out?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure which period you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Actually, I'm referring to the entire -- well, let me first limit myself, then, to 1992. In 1992, did Dr. Stakic receive Kozarski Vjesnik whenever that paper was published?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember any such papers being there. I don't know really at this time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Dr. Stakic receive the Official Gazette of the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: The Assembly was not operating at that time because the circumstances were different. The Assembly didn't meet, so there was no Official Gazette or any such material.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that the Prijedor Municipal Assembly never met in 1992 after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: They did, but I can't say when exactly. September, maybe, or thereabouts. I can't remember. August or September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us, when the Municipal Assembly was not meeting, who was leading the civilian government of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: The civilian government? The MUP, Ministry of Interior, and the army. There was no such thing as civilian government. We worked in administrative bodies. Now, what is the civilian government? The MUP, the Ministry of the Interior, if that's what you're referring to, then I should say the MUP were in charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't understand what I mean by "civilian government," or you think -- I will withdraw the question. Madam, when -- Dr. Stakic, in 1992, did he come to work every day, every day during the week?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, was he working for the government at that time or was he working for the MUP?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: He was working for the Municipal Assembly. You say "government," but I wouldn't call it government. It's an administrative body, and government is at republic level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Thank you for correcting the terminology, and please use your own terminology. I'll try to use whatever terms you use. The Municipal Assembly, just so we're clear what we're talking about --

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- the Municipal Assembly that Dr. Stakic was working for was not meeting, so who was making the decisions that were in the competence of the Municipal Assembly when it was not meeting?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Decisions in the Assembly itself you mean. I don't quite understand your question, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Decisions within the competence of the Municipal Assembly. In other words, the work that the Municipal Assembly would normally do, the decisions that they would normally make, who was making those decisions when the Municipal Assembly was not meeting in 1992?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. The Assembly wasn't meeting. There were no written decisions to be made, so I don't know. The Executive Board, the Crisis Staff, or someone. I'm not sure. Maybe that's what you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in fact, it was the Crisis Staff that took over the duties and the competencies of the Municipal Assembly. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe the witness answered but I didn't get the interpretation. Could you repeat your answer a little louder, please? The interpreters didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, among your duties sitting at the desk outside the office of the president was to bring documents for his signature or to direct them for his signature. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I never brought him any documents to be signed, not even before the war. It's just the kind of job I had. You may see my job differently from what it really was. Technical secretary, it was -- the title of my job was technical secretary. I was like a receptionist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. I'm not telling you what your job is. I'm sure you know much better than me, and we just appreciate you telling us. Isn't it a fact that you were aware, after working for many, many years with the president of the municipality of the Municipal Assembly that it was part of his job to sign the decisions of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: I know that was part of his job, yes, but I was not the one to bring them to him to be signed, myself personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for making that clear. Who would bring the documents to Dr. Stakic, after the takeover, for his signature?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: It may have been someone from a different section, the technical service of the municipality. Not the Municipal Assembly but the technical service of the municipality. That's a different service, a different unit. And I'm saying also before the war there was the same unit, because their type of work didn't change. If there was a decision to be adopted, a conclusion to be adopted, for example. And that was also the case before the war. About a rise in the prices of utilities - water, electricity, that sort of thing - then a proposal would be forwarded to this technical unit of the municipality. This technical unit, technical service would prepare this for the Assembly meeting, then they would consult with people who were qualified to discuss these subjects, and only then would they forward the proposal to the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that would be the unit headed by Mr. Baltic in 1992, Dusan Baltic; is that correct? Ma'am, if you could speak up a little bit, or perhaps if her chair could be moved closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's correct. Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And, madam, would you see, in 1992, members of that administrative service taking documents to Dr. Stakic for his signature?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't see him sign these documents, but I saw people coming. The secretary would come and say, "I need to see the president," that sort of thing. Now, what he was signing, I couldn't say. People would just bring it straight to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Having worked with Dr. Stakic for two different periods of time, would it be correct that you're familiar with his signature, the manner in which he signs his name?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm not familiar with his signature because there was never any need for me to look at his signature. I don't think I could identify his signature. I'm not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with -- I'm not asking you to recognise his signature. Are you familiar with how he would sign his name in the Latin script? Isn't it true that you saw him sign, or saw documents he signed "S. Milomir"?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your testimony is you worked with Dr. Stakic from early January 1991 until January 1993 - two years - and then in 1996 and 1997, and you don't know how he signs his name?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: She gave an answer, but I have to object to the form of the question because the question that preceded that asked if she's familiar with that specific one, but she answered the question nevertheless. But it's an inappropriate question that he asked and the follow-up was even more inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objection dismissed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, did you ever hear Dr. Stakic say that the Muslims were artificially created?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Never. I can swear a thousand times, if you'd like me to. I'll swear upon my family, if that's what it takes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already taken an oath, so I won't ask you to swear again. And you would remember that because that would be a very insulting, biased remark; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly, yes, I would remember that. I would be very disturbed by something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, you received Simo Drljaca as a visitor to Dr. Stakic during 1992. He came to his office. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I used to receive everyone who came, but Simo Drljaca never came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your testimony is that throughout 1992, you never saw Simo Drljaca in the office of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw him in June, at the beginning of June. That was the first time he came after the takeover, and I wouldn't have remembered this had they not had a fierce argument in the office, and that was the reason I remember. I had to close the window to the office so the clients waiting outside couldn't hear them quarreling, because you could hear through the open window.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was in Dr. Stakic's office?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when you answered a few moments ago, "No, I used to receive everyone who came, but Simo Drljaca never came," referring to line 3, page 88, why did you give that answer if you remember this?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. What do you mean first no and then yes? Yes. Let's just say yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in fact, ma'am, Simo Drljaca came on many more than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. Based upon that what we can read from the transcript, the Trial Chamber has decided to tell the witness about consequences on the occasion of false testimony under solemn declaration. Rule 91 of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence state: "A Chamber may warn a witness of the duty to tell the truth and the consequences that may result from a failure to do so." And your answers gave reasons to proceed this way, really to warn you to give us true answers, not to omit anything what you know. And you should be aware that when you are telling us the truth and the entire truth, you run no risk at all. But in case there is a false testimony under this solemn declaration, the Rules provide for a maximum penalty for false testimony under solemn declaration for a fine of 100.000 euros or a term of imprisonment of seven years, or both, and that is not only theory. Did you understand this admonition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did, and thank you for the warning, but I still don't know what this is all about. There may have been a misunderstanding when I answered a question. In any case, may these questions be short?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry, after your admonition I have to add something. The translation was not correct. You can check it. Page 88, line 19, the witness said, "Let's just say once," and it was translated, "Let's just say yes." So please check first with the Translation Unit and then admonish our witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please take the adequate tone here in the courtroom first; and second, the admonition was more than due. It was also based on previous testimony. So it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am surprised, because you admonish almost every single of our witnesses. You never admonish their witnesses for whom we showed 20 times that they lied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you please calm down first, and you know it is not true what you are just saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have problems with bringing our witnesses here because they heard that this Chamber is not fair toward our witnesses, and we have now problems because our people, our witnesses do not want to come here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't want to have arguments on this issue here and right now in the presence of a witness. You know this very well. If you so want, please request a 65 ter (i) meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I, since I led the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't want to go any further arguments on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's not an argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If the Prosecution can proceed and maybe, by doing so, clarify this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd just like to make an objection, if I may. To the question itself that's being asked by the OTP, that they're overly broad and not precise, and therefore, as I've objected in the past, they lack the proper foundation. Counsel is seeking questions without being specific as to a time frame, although it's rather relevant since this witness worked both prior to and subsequent to specific time periods as incorporated within the indictment. So I would just like the record to reflect that I have an ongoing and would like to be recognised as having a standing objection on the form of question because I truly believe that that is contributing in part to perhaps the answers being offered by the witness. She may be referencing a period in time that counsel is not referencing. In one question particularly he said "his." Perhaps the Court and counsel know that the question was referring to Dr. Stakic. The witness may not. The questions should be specific as they have been in the past. That's my objection, and I'm grateful that the Court has given me an opportunity to be heard on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Prosecution may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, in fact, the truth is that Mr. Drljaca was frequently in the office of Dr. Stakic in 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Not frequently. Once, I said. Once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, it was part of your job to call the members of the Crisis Staff and inform them of meetings; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was not part of my job to call the members of the Crisis Staff. And they, for that matter, did not meet anywhere in my vicinity. They would meet in the basement, in the rooms which used to house the centre for alerting people. And that's what I heard, and I did not have any need to go down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, would you call Simo Drljaca for Milomir Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: If the president had asked me to do that, I would have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry. What I'm asking you is did you in 1992 call Simo Drljaca at the request of Milomir Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't call him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, in 1992, did you see Radmilo Zeljaja in the office of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Colonels Arsic or Pero Colic in the office of the Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. In that period of time that you are referring to, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What period of time, if any, did you see Colonels Arsic and Colic in the office of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw Colic in those rooms, but I didn't go to see Stakic. I saw Colic and Arsic, and that was in 1995, but not to see Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As part of your duties, did you keep the agenda of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I did not keep the agenda of his meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it part of your duties to know where Dr. Stakic was during the day?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic would go out and would tell me, "I am here or there," or he would tell me, "I'm coming back in an hour," but it was not my duty to know where he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who would come -- who would Dr. Stakic go out with? Did you ever see him going out with other people?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "going out"? You mean outside the working hours? I don't know, after the working hours, where he went and who with.
